description: Somos AstroXplorer, un equipo multidisciplinario de Astronomía, Astrofísica e Ingeniería de Sistemas. Combinamos experiencia científica con desarrollo de software, arquitectura, análisis de datos y tecnologías web. Nos apasiona transformar datos de NASA en herramientas interactivas, útiles y científicamente rigurosas, conectando ciencia y tecnología para crear soluciones que impulsen la exploración espacial y el aprendizaje.
summary:
MarsWalker Planner is a tablet field guide for an astronaut on Mars, walking from a pressurised rover to the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp. It puts NASA data on one map to answer three questions: where a person in a suit can walk, where to stop for science, and whether to go out.

Two kinds of data decide. The terrain, from the HiRISE elevation model, sets the route: ground too steep or too rough is blocked. The radiation measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument, with NASA's DONKI space-weather forecasts, says whether to go out and when to turn back. Curiosity's photographs, rock chemistry and weather support the plan.

It matters because time outside is limited and solar storms can arrive with little warning. The guide replays a storm measured on Mars in February 2022 and shows when to return to shelter. It is a decision-support prototype, not a certified procedure.
details:
What it does

The astronaut gets one screen that leads through a walk in three steps: Plan, Check and Walk. The walk goes on foot from a pressurised rover to the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp, in Gale crater. The boxwork is a set of low ridges, 1 to 2 metres tall, with sandy hollows between them, that the Curiosity rover has explored. In Plan, the astronaut picks the shelter, which is the parked rover, and up to eight science stops. The guide draws the fastest walk that visits them. In Check, one status says GO, HOLD or NO-GO. It combines five checks: radiation, the space-weather forecast, weather and daylight, the time budget and the 30-minute shelter rule. In Walk, a simulated walk shows the next stop, the way back from here, the latest moment to turn back and the walk time. Two kinds of data are the core of the guide: the terrain and the radiation.

Core data 1: the terrain decides where a person in a suit can walk

The astronaut gets a route that keeps off ground too steep or too rough to cross in a suit. The walk zone is 2 km × 2 km, with 502 m of relief. Its shape comes from an elevation model built from HiRISE stereo images of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 1 m per pixel. The guide reads it through NASA's Mars Trek and stores it in cells of 2 m. From it the planner computes the slope over 6 m and over 10 m, and the roughness. Cells steeper than 20° or rougher than 0.50 m are blocked: about 26.6 % of the zone. Elsewhere a slope s multiplies the walking speed by exp(−3.5·|s|), the form of Tobler's hiking function, and rough ground slows it further. No validated walking speed exists for a suited astronaut on Mars, so every plan is shown at three speeds on level ground: 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 km/h. The planner tries every order of the chosen stops and keeps the fastest walk. With the example walk at 1.5 km/h, five stops make a round trip of 1,275 m. It is planned at 177 minutes of a limit of 240: the walking, 15 minutes at each stop and a 30-minute reserve.

Core data 2: the radiation decides whether to go out and when to turn back

The astronaut gets an answer before leaving and an order if the radiation rises during the walk. The measurements are the dose rates recorded on the surface of Mars by RAD, the radiation instrument of the Curiosity rover. The alert rule follows a published study of the solar particle events that RAD recorded (Löwe et al. 2025). A first measurement above 1.25 times the background raises a yellow alert. A second one confirms the event and turns the alert red. The same study says that "an astronaut should not move more than 30 min away from a shelter". So the planner keeps every point of the route within 30 minutes of walking from the shelter. Using the rule as a limit on the route is this project's own choice. Before the walk, NASA's DONKI service gives the forecast. If a simulation predicts that a coronal mass ejection will arrive at Mars within 48 hours before or after the present, the forecast check turns yellow. A forecast alone never raises a red alert.

The replay of a real solar storm

The astronaut sees what the guide does when a solar storm arrives in the middle of a walk. RAD has no live public feed, so the guide replays the dose rates that RAD measured from 15 to 18 February 2022. Every replayed value is labelled as a replay. By total dose, that event is the second largest of the 12 surface events in Table 1 of the study. The forecasts for those dates had already predicted arrivals at Mars, so the replayed walk starts under HOLD. The alert turns yellow at 22:59:31 UTC and red at 23:16:39 UTC on 15 February. The guide then says RETURN TO SHELTER, stops the clock and draws the fastest way back. With the example walk and the event beginning 90 minutes into the walk, the way back takes 11 minutes. Over the rest of the planned walk, RAD measured 20 µGy in the open (micrograys of absorbed dose). Returning then, instead of finishing the walk, avoids about 15 of them. That is an upper figure, because the shelter's shielding is not modelled.

Supporting layers

The astronaut also sees what is at each stop and what the day is like. The base map is the HiRISE image mosaic served by Mars Trek. The ten candidate stops are places where the Curiosity rover actually stood. Each shows Curiosity's Navcam photographs of the place and the ChemCam chemistry measured there. CRISM mineral composites give context for choosing stops. THEMIS thermal inertia slows the walk where the ground may be loose. REMS weather gives the daylight window. These layers are support. The data sheet lists all 15 layers, with their licence and citation. On screen, each layer that can be drawn has a plain name with its technical term beside it, such as “Uneven ground (roughness)”, and the map's scale bar gives the zone's size, 2.0 km × 2.0 km.

Other aids

The page opens on a landing that says in a few words what the guide is; beside the words, Mars drawn with characters turns and scatters when the one button, “Open the planner”, is pressed. The planner starts with no walk, so the first one is the astronaut's own: a suggested walk, or stops chosen one by one on the list or on the map. The astronaut can ask for a suggested walk and choose among four. Each is the set of stops with the most science that fits the time limit and the shelter rule: among all the stops, in half of the time limit, among the three stops with the shortest way back to the shelter, or among the two places where Curiosity drilled. The astronaut can change any stop afterwards. An elevation profile shows the height of the ground along the walk. A plan can be saved to a file and loaded again on another device. The map can fill the whole screen. A 3D view shows the relief of the zone with the rover at the shelter, and the walk can be followed from behind an astronaut who walks the route. The data layer chosen is painted on that 3D ground too, and a tap on it adds a stop or parks the shelter there. An optional guided tour of eight small windows explains each part of the screen.

How it answers the challenge

The astronaut finds on one map the things the challenge names: a route that avoids obstacles, mobility in a suit, safety and space weather, and first-person images. Here the obstacles are ground too steep or too rough, and the images are Curiosity's photographs at each stop. The challenge suggests "at least three kinds of data". The guide uses more: terrain, radiation measurements, space-weather forecasts, rover photographs, rock chemistry, mineral composites, thermal inertia and weather. The site is the example the challenge itself gives: the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp.

Benefits

The astronaut does not have to read fifteen layers to decide. A bar at the foot of Plan and of Check gives the step's answer in one line and the next action. Each check gives its reason and its data source. A check that could not be judged is named as such. The radiation check also says how often a solar particle event would start during a walk of the planned length (about 1 in 3,000 for the example walk, an estimate from the twelve events RAD recorded on the surface, Löwe et al. 2025), and it shows a radiation safety map: the ground from which the shelter is at most 30 minutes' walk away. Each of the 43 values of the model is listed as measured, published or assumption, with its source. For a visitor who is not an expert, a short card explains the three steps on the first visit, and its main button leads to the replay. A glossary explains the units and terms. The interface is in English and Spanish.

How it was checked

The astronaut can see how far the guide agrees with what a rover did on the same ground, and with the published record. Curiosity stood at 138 places inside the zone. 136 of them fall on cells the model calls walkable. The other two share one cell, where the model is stricter than the ground. At those places the mean difference between the model's local slope and the tilt the rover recorded is 0.02°, and their correlation is 0.77. On the replayed series the peak comes 3 h 55 min after the first alert, the same time to peak as in Table 1 of Löwe et al. (2025). From the first alert to the shelter the walker needs at most 47 minutes: 17 until the second measurement, then 30 of walking. That is within the lead time of 8 of the 12 events in that table, and those 8 carry 98.8 % of the summed dose of the 12. More than 900 automated tests run on the code and on the real data files. The reason for each value of the model is in docs/EVIDENCE.md in the repository.

Limits

The astronaut should take every answer of this guide as the answer of a prototype. It is a decision-support prototype, not a certified safety procedure. The radiation alert is a replay of measurements from 2022, labelled as such. RAD has no live public feed, and in live mode the radiation check is shown as not judged. The walker's position is simulated, and the guide has not been tried in the field. The walking model has not been calibrated for Mars. Its speeds, limits and times are working values: published values used by analogy (lunar suits, hikers on Earth, sand dunes) or design choices. The 20° slope limit is what NASA lists as a capability of its lunar suit, not a limit for Mars. The planner does not detect single rocks: the elevation model does not resolve them. The elevation product mixes HiRISE stereo terrain with coarser fill; inside the walk zone, a check for ground with no real detail flagged no cell. Thermal inertia has pixels of 100 m, far wider than the ridges. No dose shown counts the protection of the shelter.

Tools and languages

The astronaut, or any visitor, needs only a browser. The guide is a static web page, and its prepared data travel with it. The only request it makes to another site is the live forecast, to api.nasa.gov. If the service cannot be reached, a bundled snapshot is used and labelled with its date. The code is plain JavaScript, with no framework. The map is drawn with Leaflet 1.9.4, and the 3D view with three.js 0.187.0. The site is built with Vite 8.3.8, on Node.js 22.12 or newer. The data tools read GeoTIFF files with geotiff.js 3.0.5. The code is released under the Apache License 2.0, and the data keep their own licences.

Repository: https://github.com/RALC365/nasa-space-challenge-2026

How it was built

The team's physicist chose the place and the science goal, the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, and wrote the physical assumptions of the model with their references. The search that finds the route began in AstroXplorer, the first version of this project, built by a member of the team. The ideas of the full-screen map, the elevation profile, saving a plan, the suggested walk and the 3D view come from two members' own prototypes and from the team's meeting. The project coordinator asked that the walker in the 3D view be a figure of a person who walks, and the rover an object, not map glyphs, and then for other routes, to give the exploration more diversity. After seeing the product, the team asked that the page open with no walk, so that a route already drawn is not taken for the only one, and for an optional guided tour.

The code and the documents were written with AI tools (Claude Code, by Anthropic), which the Space Apps guides call Super Intelligence (SI), under the team's direction. The application itself makes no AI calls and holds no AI-generated audio or data. Its two logos, the project's and the team's, are AI-generated images, made by the team mainly with Codex (OpenAI); each carries a label that says so. The planet drawn with characters on the landing was made by a member of the team with an AI tool, and adapted to this product. The demo video was assembled with AI tools from a recording of the running application, and it says so on screen. What AI did, what people decided and how the results were checked are in docs/AI_USE.md in the repository, the only page that deals with it.
